request: Allocate the next one-step retrosynthesis call for an acetanilide planning tree under Retro*. Open node A has local remaining estimate 0.1, ancestor reaction cost sum 0.2, and unresolved off-path sibling cost sum 9. Open node B has corresponding values 2, 1, and 1. No other frontier exists. Which call should the best-first policy make?

options.A: Expand A because its own remaining estimate is smallest.
options.B: Expand B because it belongs to the cheaper complete target plan estimate.
options.C: Expand both as a mandatory batch.

request: Choose the next promising root reaction for an ester target. Reaction R1 costs 0.2 and requires BOTH precursor branches with estimates 0.1 and 8. Reaction R2 costs 1.2 and has a single precursor with estimate 3. Costs use one common additive surrogate and neither reaction has yet been validated experimentally.

options.A: Prefer R1 using its cheapest precursor only.
options.B: Prefer R1 solely because its one-step cost is lower.
options.C: Prefer R2 after summing all obligations within each reaction.

request: For the pinned Retro* default search objective, the target is CC(=O)Nc1ccccc1. A required precursor Nc1ccccc1 is already in starting_mols, but value_fn returns 7 for it. How should this precursor enter the search state?

options.A: Known, closed, success=true, remaining synthesis cost 0.
options.B: Open until the value network returns zero.
options.C: Known but carrying predicted remaining cost 7 in the default tree.

request: Current target ancestry on this branch is T -> A -> B. Expanding B proposes a reaction requiring C. C appeared under a different alternative branch but is not T, A, or B. There is no graph-sharing implementation; this is the original tree policy. What should happen?

options.A: Reject because C was ever seen anywhere.
options.B: Reject because all repeated structures prove a chemical cycle.
options.C: Retain the proposal; a molecule in another branch is not an ancestor cycle.

request: The fixed top-k one-step model returns no candidates when expanding an unavailable precursor. Another root alternative is still open. What conclusion and search action are justified?

options.A: The target is chemically impossible; end all search.
options.B: Mark this attempted branch exhausted at infinite estimated cost, propagate, and consider other open alternatives.
options.C: Give the branch zero cost because no reaction is required.

request: Reproduce default score-to-reaction-cost behavior of the pinned binghong-ml/retro_star implementation, not an idealized variant. Two supplied one-step scores are 0 and 0.0005. Which costs should the planner assign?

options.A: Both approximately 6.907755 because the implementation clips to a common lower floor before negative log.
options.B: Infinity and approximately 7.600902, using an unclipped negative log.
options.C: Zero and 0.0005; raw scores are costs.

request: A Retro* run returns its first complete route with cost 7. A learned value network guided the search; admissibility has not been established and an open alternative has estimated root cost 3. Can the agent certify this route globally minimum-cost?

options.A: Yes, every algorithm called A* guarantees it even with arbitrary learned values.
options.B: Yes, completion alone is a lower-bound certificate.
options.C: No; report a found route and distinguish it from an optimality certificate under appropriate lower-bound assumptions.

request: A completed tree route is cheapest under summed negative log one-step model scores. The user now asks which route has the highest measured yield under humidity-sensitive scale-up conditions. No experimental condition or yield data are available. What is supported?

options.A: Treat minimum score-cost as highest measured yield.
options.B: State that the surrogate ranking does not answer the new objective and obtain relevant condition/yield evidence.
options.C: Convert exp(-route_cost) directly into an experimental yield.

request: Reproduce prepare_test_prediction.py in the pinned uta-smile/RetroXpert implementation. In an existing three-bond product chain, the flattened adjacency prediction entries are [0.82,0.82,0.09,0.09,0.35,0.35], with consecutive pairs corresponding to both directions of bonds b1,b2,b3. The predicted disconnection count is 1; diagnostic ground truth count is 2. Which physical bond set should inference disconnect?

options.C: b2 and b3, using the diagnostic ground-truth count.

request: For the same pinned RetroXpert adjacency-log decoding, paired entries for b1,b2,b3,b4 are [0.9,0.9,0.3,0.3,0.7,0.7,0.1,0.1]. The predicted physical bond disconnection count is 2. Which result matches the implementation?

options.A: Remove b4 alone because two selected matrix positions are one bond.
options.B: Remove b1 and b3 using highest adjacency scores.
options.C: Select four lowest directed positions, corresponding to b2 and b4.

request: RetroXpert's auxiliary classifier predicts zero disconnections for a test product. Several adjacency scores are small. No alternative count hypotheses were requested. Which behavior follows the count-guided default decoding policy?

options.A: Cut no bonds in this decoding pass; zero is a valid count class, not a command to force the smallest score.
options.B: Always disconnect one bond to produce a retrosynthesis.
options.C: Use the hidden test reaction to choose how many cuts to make.

request: A two-stage retrosynthesis model predicts reactants well with reference synthons but poorly with its own predicted synthons. The EGAT training split has labeled reactions and erroneous predicted centers. Which targeted RGN training intervention follows RetroXpert's stated robustness method?

options.A: Train only on perfectly predicted centers, removing error cases.
options.B: Add failed training-set predicted synthons paired with their reference reactants, without reversing those error-augmentation examples.
options.C: Replace training targets with predicted synthons and add labeled test errors to training.

request: A clean RGN training record has input product + synthon S1.S2, and mapped overlap establishes targets R1.R2 corresponding to S1.S2. Create the clean order-augmentation counterpart. What pairing is correct?

options.A: S2.S1 -> R1.R2, keeping the old target order.

request: After the prescribed bond split, an intermediate synthon is representable for the RGN but is not a chemically valid stable purchasable molecule under ordinary molecule sanitization. The original paper explicitly permits this intermediate representation. Which handling is appropriate?

options.A: Keep it as a scoped intermediate for reactant completion; validate final reactants separately and do not present the synthon as an isolated reagent.
options.B: Delete every such intermediate before RGN because synthons must be stable reagents.
options.C: Report the synthon directly as a final purchasable reactant.

request: An unpaired new product has no known reactants or atom correspondence. A proposed deployment patch copies the training routine that aligns targets to synthons using overlap with ground-truth reactant atom maps. What should the agent do?

options.A: Invent reference reactant atom maps to retain the training routine unchanged.
options.B: Use training-only target alignment only where labels exist; do not require unavailable ground-truth reactants for product-only inference.
options.C: Read held-out answers and expose their ordering to the deployed predictor.

request: The error-augmented RGN was trained on its EGAT's in-distribution failures. A new upstream center predictor makes qualitatively different mistakes on a different chemistry domain. Does the original error-augmentation result certify recovery here?

options.A: Yes, augmentation guarantees correction of arbitrary center errors.
options.B: Yes, the chemical domain never affects the error distribution.
options.C: No; validate this changed error distribution and obtain representative training evidence before claiming recovery.
